The Seam and the Seat

Two open-loop results in this program had never met: the reorientation that stands a shaft up in the hand, and the gait that spins one already standing on the floor. Joining them turns out to be a race against a grasp that leaks. Then the floating palm is replaced by a UR5e, and the floor by a countersink.

What was already true

two open-loop results, neither with any claim on the other

probe_real_v1_carry.py takes the shaft off the table and stands it vertical in the hand: a fixed grasp, a rotation about a pivot raised above the contacts, cos 0.996, no policy anywhere. probe_real_v1_gait.py spins a shaft that is already standing on the floor through five revolutions in forty four-phase cycles, again from a precomputed set-point table. The first ends with the tool in the air at 113 mm; the second begins with it planted at 50 mm, put there by a line of code.

Everything below is about the 63 mm in between, and then about replacing the two conveniences that made both results possible: a palm that can be commanded to any pose, and a floor that is a flat plane.

The chain

grasp → lift → reorient → set down → release → re-index → gait

One rollout, one MjData, no state passed through a file. The re-pose is written as a rigid transfer — if the tool rides in the palm frame then asking for an object pose fully determines the palm pose, T_palm = T_obj_des · T_obj-1 · T_palm — because that is the form an arm can be handed later. Every phase below carries the time since the grasp closed, the pad force at that moment, and the tool's tilt from vertical.

01lifted1.3 s · 5.6 N · 89.9°
02reoriented3.4 s · 12.0 N · 4.8°
03set down4.4 s · 5.5 N · 10.5°
04upright7.6 s · 1.2 N · 0.5°
05pressed9.0 s · 0.4 N · 0.5°
06released9.4 s · 0.0 N · 0.0°
07reindexed11.4 s · 0.0 N · 0.0°
08gait grip12.8 s · 26.9 N · 0.3°
09gaited18.6 s · 26.8 N · 1.2°

Success is the conjunction of four gates, not the cosine: the carry held, the tool stood within 10 mm of its resting height with support contact and under 14° of tilt, the gait grasp took on at least two pads, and all requested cycles ran without the tool being lost. A run that reoriented beautifully and then dropped the shaft on the way down reads false.

Only rv05_manual_stored — the hand the bench was built from — completes. The other nine fail at the carry, and they fail under rv05's published carry settings applied unchanged: axis height, turn duration and residual budget were never re-tuned per design. That is a statement about this experiment, not about those hands.

The seam is a race

what the carry hands over, and how long it lasts

The carry does not end in a grip. At the top of a raised-pivot turn the tool is commonly cradled against the middle phalanges with the pads barely on it — about half a millimetre of commanded interference — and that hold leaks. The shaft creeps down through the pads at roughly 1.5 mm/s and the pad force decays to nothing in under two seconds, which probe_real_v1_carry already measured from the other direction (16.1 N to zero, tool on the table by 1.6 s).

Two consequences follow, and the second is the one worth keeping.

Feedback on the height is harmful. The set-down is driven by re-measuring the tool and recomputing the palm pose. Doing that once, as a single continuous move, stands the tool on 6 of 6 spawn-jittered seeds. Doing it eight times stands it on 1. Nothing about the trajectory changes — the extra corrections only add dwells, and every dwell is paid in grip. The height error being corrected is the slip, and lowering the palm further does not put it back.

Feedback on the tilt is not. The same loop applied to orientation is harmless at any number of corrections, because a rotation about the tool's own foot does not trade against the grip in the same way.

The controls

conditionchains turnsnote
full chain, as shipped6/60.98the reference
no floor during the gait0/60.00floor deleted after the gait grasp is set
gait from the carry's own grip1/61.90no release, no re-index; ring solved at the carry's palm pose
change grasp in mid-air0/60.00take the gait's ring before setting down; it solves to 1.1 mm

The mid-air re-grasp is the one that changed how I think about the floor. The gait's tripod ring solves to 1.1 mm at the carry's own palm pose — it is reachable, and the fingers can hold it — but a linear joint-space move from one grasp to the other passes through a configuration that holds neither, and in mid-air there is nothing under the tool. Set it on the floor first and the identical transition works every time. The floor's contribution is not only that a released tool stays put; it is that the hand becomes free to change its mind about how to hold it.

What the seam will absorb

The carry's exit tilt depends almost entirely on how long the hold after the turn is allowed to run — cos 0.837 at the last commanded step, 0.946 after 0.6 s, 0.996 after 1.0. Handing the seam anything from 6° to 25° makes no difference to whether the chain completes.

The gait itself keeps the ceiling it had on a bare floor: 30° of azimuth per cycle is safe, 45° roughly doubles throughput at a real cost in reliability, and 60° walks the tool over.

Read the 45° row carefully. The pad ring is a gear — the pads ride at 21.05 mm about a 12.5 mm shaft, so slip-free transmission is 1.684 — and 1.684 × 45° is 75.8°. The measured 91° per cycle is 1.20 times that ceiling, which means the tool is being flicked and left to coast rather than driven. That is throughput of a kind, but it is not the same primitive, and the reliability drop is where it shows.

On an arm

the six palm DOF, paid for by a UR5e

Every number this program has produced was made by a floating, gravity-compensated palm carrying six position-actuated joints. build_real_v1_arm_scene.py deletes them and bolts the hand to a UR5e flange; palm_driver.py puts the gantry and the arm behind one read / write / solve / cmd_pose interface, so the chain probe contains no branch on which wrist it is using and a difference between the two runs belongs to the wrist. Differential IK is mink, pinned to 1.1 — 1.2 resolves MuJoCo to 3.12, and every physics result in this repository was measured on 3.6. The solver runs on a separate arm-only model, because mink integrates over every degree of freedom a model has and the task scene's include nine finger joints and the tool's free joint.

The arm is not worse. Worst IK residual over a whole rollout is a thousandth of a millimetre and no commanded pose was unreachable, so the palm trajectory the seam needs is not exotic — a 6R arm makes all of it, including the rigid re-pose transfer and the lateral re-index under a standing tool.

What the arm costs is stiffness, and it is a cliff rather than a slope. The menagerie UR5e has no gravity feedforward: its shoulder sits 21 mrad below its set-point under the arm's own twelve kilograms, and the palm droops 12.7 mm at the top of the lift. That alone turns a 5° carry exit into 29° and breaks the seam. Compensating the arm's links — not the hand, which is real payload the controller does not know about — sweeps that droop continuously from 12.7 mm down to 0.35 mm on an otherwise identical robot.

the spec

A wrist for this task has to hold the commanded palm pose to about one millimetre under the hand's own weight plus a 25 g tool. That is a number an arm can be checked against before it is bought, and it is the first hardware requirement this program has stated in units that are not the hand's own.

Into a screw

a 45° frustum tip, and a countersink to put it in

A flat-ended rod on a flat plane makes the ground a pure friction brake and leaves the tool free to walk, which is why drift_mm had to be reported at all. A screw sits in a seat, and a seat centres, wedges and constrains. The tool gains a 45° frustum tip — a mesh, so the cone is exact rather than stepped, and a frustum is convex so MuJoCo's hull is the shape itself — and the floor gains a matching countersink. A conical hole is not convex, so the seat is built the way a real recess is: a ring of thirty-two facets for the wall, a disc for the relieved bottom, and a flat annulus for the table around the mouth.

The tool is picked up lying on the table, 40 mm from the seat, so the chain has to transport it as well as insert it.

The seat costs 49.0 → 40.3 degrees per cycle, about a sixth of the turn, and returns 1.28 → 0.08 mm of walk, a factor of sixteen. The loss is the wedge: normal force on a cone flank is the axial load over sin α, so the same press buys more resisting torque than it does on a plane. Over forty cycles the seated tool turns 4.44 revolutions against 5.11 on the plane, and stays seated.

The cone angle trades those two against each other directly, and the ratio is the wedge factor read off the data: 2.00, 1.41, 1.15 for half-angles of 30, 45 and 60 degrees.

Insertion is a press, not a placement

Below about 8 mm of commanded press the tip stops proud of its seat and the gait has nothing to push against; from 10 to 18 mm there is no further change. And the capture radius is 6 mm against 10.5 mm of geometric clearance, because the tool arrives with two to five degrees of tilt and a tilted cone binds in a matched cone — an 8° entry stops three millimetres into a ten-millimetre seat.

The re-grip that pays for the insertion has a narrow window of its own. Too little and the grasp is gone before the tip is home; too much and the pads, which sit at different stations along the shaft, torque it out of line and the cone binds on the way in.

Transport distance, by contrast, does not matter. Standing the tool up and carrying it across are expressed as one pose command and therefore one ramp, so 30 mm and 90 mm cost the same.

What this does and does not show

It is simulation, on one hand, with one tool. The upright starting pose is produced by the carry rather than granted, which was the point, but the carry itself is rv05's published configuration and the other nine designs never reach the seam under it. Nothing here has been through the trajectory-clearance or servo-limit gates, so none of it is a deployment claim. A 45° countersink at 0.0072 N·m of resisting torque is a seat, not a fastener — there is no thread, no pitch, and the tool does not have to descend as it turns.

Three measurement errors on the way each read as physics before a control caught them, and they are recorded because two of them are the same error in different clothes. A re-grip measured from the pad's achieved position hands back exactly the deflection that was carrying the load, and bled a “constant” grip from 18.4 N to 0.25 N over seven reissues with the tool doing nothing; the bench work met this one as achieved_fraction. A proportional tilt correction tracking a scheduled reference changes sign whenever the plant runs behind, and on a 20 N grip with 150 steps of lag it always does — the palm oscillated to −0.49 rad and threw the tool from a state that had already reached 3°. And probe_real_v1_gait._ground asks for contacts with the body named world, which reports zero support for a tool sitting firmly in a seat that is its own body.

Next

  • Put the seat on a load cell in sim: sweep resisting torque until the gait stalls, and report the stall torque rather than the turn rate. That number is what decides whether this is a fastener primitive.
  • Close the gait loop. Gaiting is the first task in this program whose controlled variable — rotation about the tool's own axis — the bench's AprilTag rig measures directly, at 0.017° rms.
  • Run the export and clearance gates on the chained trajectory. The gait's ring grasp and the re-index move have never been checked against finger–finger clearance or the servo travel limits, and three of four plans on the control station once failed exactly that check.

Reproduce

uv run --extra rl python scripts/real_v1_chain_study.py \
    --out docs/experiments/20260903-real_v1_chain --reps 6 --cycles 8

uv run --extra rl --extra arm python scripts/build_real_v1_arm_scene.py
uv run --extra rl --extra arm python scripts/real_v1_arm_study.py \
    --out docs/experiments/20260903-real_v1_chain --reps 6 --cycles 8

uv run --extra rl python scripts/real_v1_screw_study.py \
    --out docs/experiments/20260903-real_v1_screw --reps 6 --cycles 8

uv run --extra rl python scripts/real_v1_chain_page.py

Each study is well under a minute of CPU on six workers; the arm study is serial because mink holds a model per process.
